content: Gliclazide is an oral medication used to lower blood sugar levels and is classified as a sulfonylurea. It is commercially available under the brand name Diamicron MR®, as well as other names such as Diabeton MR, Diamicron 30mg, Diamicron LM 30mg, Diamicron MR 30 mg, Diamicron Uno 30mg, Dianormax MR, Diaprel MR, and Uni Diamicron. However, it is not marketed in the United States. Each tablet of gliclazide contains 80 mg of the active ingredient. The drug is indicated for the management of hyperglycemia in patients with stable, mild, non-ketosis-prone, maturity-onset (adult-type) diabetes mellitus who are responsive to gliclazide. It is prescribed when proper dietary management and exercise fail to control blood sugar levels or when insulin therapy is deemed inappropriate. The dosage of gliclazide ranges from 40 mg to 240 mg daily, depending on the patient’s response. It is typically taken once or twice daily before meals, with a maximum single dose of 160 mg. Gliclazide works as a hypoglycemic sulfonylurea by restoring the first phase of insulin secretion and increasing insulin sensitivity. It also exhibits glycemia-independent hemovascular effects and has antioxidant properties. Importantly, it does not produce active circulating metabolites. The drug is contraindicated in patients with type 1 diabetes, hypersensitivity to sulfonylureas, severe renal or hepatic failure, and during pregnancy or lactation. It is also contraindicated when co-prescribed with miconazole. Certain drug interactions may affect gliclazide’s efficacy. For instance, its blood sugar-lowering effect may be reduced by medications such as danazol, chlorpromazine, glucocorticoids, progestogens, and β-2 agonists. Conversely, its hypoglycemic action may be enhanced by drugs like phenylbutazone, alcohol, fluconazole, β-blockers, and possibly ACE inhibitors. Adverse effects associated with gliclazide include hypoglycemia, gastrointestinal disturbances (commonly reported), rare skin reactions, rare hematological disorders, and exceptionally rare elevations in hepatic enzymes. In cases of overdose, severe hypoglycemia may occur, necessitating urgent administration of intravenous glucose and close monitoring of the patient.
